families.name: Fried Liver Attack
families.idea: The sharp answer to the Two Knights: 4.Ng5 hits f7 twice. If Black recaptures on d5 with the knight, sacrifice on f7 and drag the king into the middle. Against the real refutations (5...Na5, 5...b5, 5...Nd4, the Traxler) know the one calm reply to each.
masters: The sacrifice is old: it appears in the Italian manuscripts of Giulio Cesare Polerio around 1600, and the Italian name Fegatello is usually translated as fried liver.
6.d4 is named after the 18th-century Italian writer Giambattista Lolli, and 4...Bc5 after the Czech priest and chess problemist Karel Traxler.
Engines rate 4.Ng5 as one of White's most testing tries against the Two Knights, though 5...Na5 holds the balance.

friedliver.name: Fried Liver Attack
friedliver.idea: Against the Two Knights, 4.Ng5 attacks f7 twice. If Black takes back on d5 with the knight, sacrifice on f7, check on f3 and pile up on the pinned knight. The black king ends up in the middle while yours castles.
notes: Centre pawn: open lines for the queen and bishop.
Develop with a threat on e5.
The Two Knights: Black hits e4 instead of playing ...Bc5.
Knight to g5: two pieces on f7.
The mistake: the knight becomes a target.
The Fried Liver: sacrifice on f7.
Check, and d5 is hit twice.
Pile up on the pinned knight.
why: You claim the centre and free your queen and f1-bishop. Against 1...e5 this pawn is the one Black attacks most, so a lot of the Italian is about keeping e4 secure while you develop.
Black takes the same central share and frees the f8-bishop. The e5 pawn becomes your first target, and you attack it with developing moves rather than pawn moves so that each one gains time.
You develop with a threat on e5, so Black must answer. The knight on f3 also covers d4 and prepares castling. This is the move order of every line in the family, so Black's real choices start next.
Black protects e5 with a developing move. The knight on c6 eyes d4, which means your d4 break later will usually need c3 first. It is the most common reply and keeps all of Black's options open.
The bishop targets f7, the square only Black's king protects, and clears f1 so you can castle. Against this bishop, Black must decide between mirroring with ...Bc5 and counterattacking with ...Nf6.
The Two Knights Defence: instead of copying you, Black develops and attacks e4 straight away. Nothing defends e4, so you must either protect it or start a fight with the sharp 4.Ng5 or 4.d4.

The knight moves a second time to join the c4-bishop against f7, which only the black king defends. The threat is Nxf7, forking queen and rook. Black has to answer at once, and every answer leads to a different fight, so this is the move that starts all your preparation.

Three times in four, Black blocks the bishop's diagonal with d5. It is the right idea: it cuts the c4-bishop off from f7 and opens the c8-bishop. Now the question is how Black takes back after you capture.

Take. The pawn on d5 now stands in your own bishop's way, but it is a pawn, and Black has to decide how to win it back. Knight takes is the natural move and the mistake. Knight to a5 is the main line and the best.

Knight takes d5 looks natural and loses the right to castle. The knight blocks its own bishop from defending f7, and it will be pinned to the king on d5. This is the move the Fried Liver waits for, and it is played in almost half the games under 1800.

Knight takes f7, forking queen and rook. Black has to take back with the king, and that king is then dragged into the middle. You give a knight for a pawn and a long attack. Stockfish rates it about plus 0.9.
The king takes; anything else leaves Black a pawn down with the rook or queen lost. Now the king stands on f7 with the d5-knight in front of it, and both are about to be hit.

Queen to f3 gives check and hits the d5-knight a second time, with the bishop. The knight cannot be guarded by a piece in time, so the king has to help. Watch where it goes: each king move has its own punishment.
Ke6 is Black's best and is found only about a third of the time under 1800. The king guards d5 itself, and the knight there is now pinned against it by your bishop.
Knight to c3 attacks d5 a third time. The pinned knight cannot move, so Black has to keep finding defenders.
Knight to b4 guards d5 once more and eyes the fork on c2. Other knight moves lose quickly: after Nce7, d4 opens the centre and Stockfish gives about plus three.
Castle and keep your king safe while Black's stays in the middle. Old books play a3 or Qe4 here, and both are mistakes: a3 is met by Nxc2+ forking king and rook, and Stockfish then prefers Black.
Black props up d5 with a pawn. The king is still on e6 in front of all its pawns.

d4 attacks e5 and opens lines towards the king on e6, while freeing your c1-bishop. You are a piece down for a pawn and Stockfish still prefers you, about plus 0.7. Keep bringing pieces: Re1, Bg5 or Bf4.

friedliver-ke7.name: Fried Liver trap: 7...Ke7
friedliver-ke7.idea: If the king goes to e7, win the knight back and give check on f7. The king is driven to d6 with no shelter.
notes: Centre pawn: open lines for the queen and bishop.
Develop with a threat on e5.
The Two Knights: Black hits e4 instead of playing ...Bc5.
Knight to g5: two pieces on f7.
The mistake: the knight becomes a target.
The Fried Liver: sacrifice on f7.
Check, and d5 is hit twice.
The king steps up to e7.
why: You claim the centre and free your queen and f1-bishop. Against 1...e5 this pawn is the one Black attacks most, so a lot of the Italian is about keeping e4 secure while you develop.
Black takes the same central share and frees the f8-bishop. The e5 pawn becomes your first target, and you attack it with developing moves rather than pawn moves so that each one gains time.
You develop with a threat on e5, so Black must answer. The knight on f3 also covers d4 and prepares castling. This is the move order of every line in the family, so Black's real choices start next.
Black protects e5 with a developing move. The knight on c6 eyes d4, which means your d4 break later will usually need c3 first. It is the most common reply and keeps all of Black's options open.
The bishop targets f7, the square only Black's king protects, and clears f1 so you can castle. Against this bishop, Black must decide between mirroring with ...Bc5 and counterattacking with ...Nf6.
The Two Knights Defence: instead of copying you, Black develops and attacks e4 straight away. Nothing defends e4, so you must either protect it or start a fight with the sharp 4.Ng5 or 4.d4.

The knight moves a second time to join the c4-bishop against f7, which only the black king defends. The threat is Nxf7, forking queen and rook. Black has to answer at once, and every answer leads to a different fight, so this is the move that starts all your preparation.

Three times in four, Black blocks the bishop's diagonal with d5. It is the right idea: it cuts the c4-bishop off from f7 and opens the c8-bishop. Now the question is how Black takes back after you capture.

Take. The pawn on d5 now stands in your own bishop's way, but it is a pawn, and Black has to decide how to win it back. Knight takes is the natural move and the mistake. Knight to a5 is the main line and the best.

Knight takes d5 looks natural and loses the right to castle. The knight blocks its own bishop from defending f7, and it will be pinned to the king on d5. This is the move the Fried Liver waits for, and it is played in almost half the games under 1800.

Knight takes f7, forking queen and rook. Black has to take back with the king, and that king is then dragged into the middle. You give a knight for a pawn and a long attack. Stockfish rates it about plus 0.9.
The king takes; anything else leaves Black a pawn down with the rook or queen lost. Now the king stands on f7 with the d5-knight in front of it, and both are about to be hit.

Queen to f3 gives check and hits the d5-knight a second time, with the bishop. The knight cannot be guarded by a piece in time, so the king has to help. Watch where it goes: each king move has its own punishment.
King to e7 leaves d5 defended only once.
Bishop takes d5. Material is level and the king is still in the middle.
The knight jumps at your queen with tempo.
Ignore the threat and give check on f7. The king has to walk forward.
The king stands on d6 with no shelter. Stockfish gives about plus three: bring the knight with Na3 and Nc4+.

friedliver-exd4.name: Fried Liver trap: 10...exd4
friedliver-exd4.idea: In the main line, taking on d4 opens the e-file in front of the black king, and the rook joins with check.

Pile up on the pinned knight.

Ke6 is Black's best and is found only about a third of the time under 1800. The king guards d5 itself, and the knight there is now pinned against it by your bishop.
Knight to c3 attacks d5 a third time. The pinned knight cannot move, so Black has to keep finding defenders.
Knight to b4 guards d5 once more and eyes the fork on c2. Other knight moves lose quickly: after Nce7, d4 opens the centre and Stockfish gives about plus three.
Castle and keep your king safe while Black's stays in the middle. Old books play a3 or Qe4 here, and both are mistakes: a3 is met by Nxc2+ forking king and rook, and Stockfish then prefers Black.
Black props up d5 with a pawn. The king is still on e6 in front of all its pawns.

d4 attacks e5 and opens lines towards the king on e6, while freeing your c1-bishop. You are a piece down for a pawn and Stockfish still prefers you, about plus 0.7. Keep bringing pieces: Re1, Bg5 or Bf4.
Taking on d4 opens the e-file right in front of the black king.
The rook comes in with check. The king has no shelter, and your bishops and queen join next. Stockfish gives about plus four and more as it looks deeper.
